chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Dawud al-Raqqi, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'May I be sacrificed for you! A man from the companions of Abu al-Khattab forbade eating al-Bukht and eating the meat of al-Masruwalah pigeons.' So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no problem with riding al-Bukht, drinking their milk, and eating the meat of al-Masruwalah pigeons.'

key_terms.أَصْحَابِ أَبِي الْخَطَّابِ: The companions of Abu al-Khattab (a known jurist or narrator)
key_terms.الْبُخْت: A specific type of camel, often described as strutting or racing camels
key_terms.الْحَمَامِ الْمُسَرْوَلَةِ: A specific type of pigeon, characterized by its gait or appearance
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ: There is no problem / It is permissible

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on eating Bukht camels and Masruwalah pigeons in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith illustrates the principle of *al-asl fi al-ashya' al-ibahah* (the default ruling for things is permissibility) by correcting a specific local custom or over-caution of the companions of Abu al-Khattab. Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies that while these animals were subject to prohibition in certain contexts, their meat, milk, and utility remain fundamentally lawful (*halal*), emphasizing the distinction between cultural aversion and jurisprudential ruling.
